Viyalamak: To bring the rudder back so that the ship's head stays on the ordered course; the order 'Viya!' (Steady!) tells the helmsman to hold the ship's head steady on that course.
Küpeşte: The solid rail or plating along the edge of the deck; it stops people on board from falling overboard.
Borda: The side shell of the ship; referred to as the port side or the starboard side.
İskele (Port): The left-hand side of the ship looking forward; shown at night by the red sidelight.
Sancak: The right-hand side of the ship looking forward; shown at night by the green sidelight.
Pruva: The forward end of the ship, shaped to part the water and meet the waves.
Kıç: The after end of the ship, where the rudder and the propeller are located.
Omurga (Keel): The main structural member running fore and aft along the bottom of the ship; the backbone of the hull.
Postalar (Frames): Transverse structural members fitted at right angles to the keel; they give the hull its shape.
Güverte (Deck): A horizontal level of the ship; used for walking, working and carrying cargo.
Ambar (Hold): An enclosed space below deck for carrying cargo.
Sintine (Bilge): The lowest part of the inside of the hull, between the keel and the ship's side, where leakage water collects.
Baca (Funnel): The structure that carries the engine room exhaust gases out of the ship; its colours also identify the shipping company.
Köprü Üstü (Bridge): The ship's command centre: the enclosed space that houses the navigation, manoeuvring and communication equipment.
Kamarot: A crew member responsible for looking after and cleaning passenger or crew cabins.
Lostromo (Bosun): The senior deck rating; in charge of rope work, painting and deck maintenance.
Vardiya: The period of duty kept by the ship's personnel; usually organised as four hours on and eight hours off (4-8) or six on and six off (6-6).
Alabanda: Turning the rudder to its maximum angle; given as the orders 'hard a-port' or 'hard a-starboard'.
Apiko: The moment when the anchor cable is vertical and the anchor is about to break out of the seabed.
Baş Bodoslama: The structural member at the very fore end of the bow, rising vertically from the keel.
Kıç Bodoslama: The structural member at the after end, rising vertically from the keel.
Borda Feneri: The navigation lights on the port and starboard sides of the ship; red to port, green to starboard.
Çarmık: Ropes or wires set up between the mast and the ship's side to support the mast; ratlines on them let the crew climb aloft.
Matafora: A crane-like mechanical arrangement used to lower lifeboats and rescue boats into the water.
Karakol: The watch kept to look out for anything affecting the safe navigation of the ship.
Grandi: The main sail, usually the largest sail, set on the mainmast.
Flama: A long, narrow flag used for signalling.
Çıma: The free end of a rope, the part that is moved when making a knot or passing the line.
Babafingo: On square-rigged sailing ships, the sail set above the topsail, high up on the mast.
Bocurgat (Windlass): The machine on the forecastle used to heave in and pay out the anchor cable.
Palamar: The general name for the ropes used to make the ship fast to a berth or a buoy.
Kaptan Köşkü: The part of the bridge where the master stands and the navigation orders are given.
Çamaşırlık: The space where the crew wash their clothes; a separate compartment on large ships.
Karantina Bayrağı: The yellow flag Q; it means 'My vessel is healthy and I request free pratique'. An arriving ship flies it until pratique is granted.
Volta: Securing a rope by taking turns around a bollard or bitts.
Bağ (Knot): A fastening made by tying a rope to itself or to another rope.
Ek (Splice): A permanent join made by interweaving the strands of rope ends.
Kasa Bağı: A splice that forms a permanent eye (loop) at the end of a rope.
Camadan: Reducing the area of a sail by gathering in part of it and tying it down; the flat knot used for this is the reef knot.
Palanga: A combination of blocks and rope used to multiply the pulling force.
Makara (Block): A sheave in a frame through which a rope runs; it changes the direction of the pull or, combined in a tackle, multiplies it.
Kıstırma (Stopper): A device used to hold a rope or chain under load, so that it can be transferred to bitts or a cleat.
Yeke: The lever used to turn the rudder by hand; used for direct steering on small boats.
Baba (Bollard): A short, strong vertical post on a quay or on board to which mooring lines are made fast.
Bite (Bitt): A pair of strong posts on deck around which mooring lines are turned up.
Sapan (Sling): A wire or synthetic rope arrangement used to attach a load to a lifting hook.
Mevki (Position): The location of a ship at a given moment, expressed in latitude and longitude.
DGPS: Differential GPS: satellite positioning improved to metre or better accuracy by corrections from reference stations.
Kerteriz (Bearing): The direction from the observer to an object; measured with a compass and expressed in degrees.
Rota (Course): The direction in which the ship is steered or is planned to go; measured clockwise from north.
Büyük Daire Seyri (Great Circle): Sailing along the arc of a great circle, which is the shortest distance between two points on the Earth's surface.
Loksodrom (Rhumb Line): A line that crosses every meridian at the same angle; the track followed when the compass course is not changed.
Meridyen: An imaginary half circle running from the North Pole to the South Pole; it defines longitude.
Paralel: An imaginary circle running parallel to the equator; it defines latitude.
Enlem (Latitude): The angular distance of a place north or south of the equator, measured from 0° to 90°.
Boylam (Longitude): The angular distance of a place east or west of the Greenwich meridian, measured from 0° to 180°.
Deniz Mili (Nautical Mile): The unit of distance equal to one minute of arc of latitude; 1852 metres.
Knot: The unit of speed at sea: one nautical mile per hour.
ETA (Estimated Time of Arrival): The time at which the ship is expected to arrive at a port or a given position.
ETD (Estimated Time of Departure): The time at which the ship is expected to leave port.
AIS (Automatic Identification System): A radio system that automatically transmits the ship's identity, position, course and speed.
ECDIS: Electronic Chart Display and Information System; when it meets the carriage rules it is accepted as equivalent to paper charts.
Radar: Equipment that uses radio waves to detect the position, range and movement of surrounding objects.
ARPA: Automatic Radar Plotting Aid; automatically works out the course, speed and closest point of approach of tracked targets.
CPA (Closest Point of Approach): The predicted smallest distance at which two ships will pass each other.
TCPA (Time to CPA): The predicted time remaining until two ships reach their closest point of approach.
Pusula Hatası (Compass Error): The total difference between the north shown by the compass and true north; the sum of variation and deviation.
Sapma (Variation): The angle between true north and magnetic north; it changes with geographical position.
İnhiraf (Deviation): The difference between magnetic north and compass north, caused by the ship's own iron and steel.
Seyir Planı (Passage Plan): A detailed berth-to-berth plan prepared so that the ship can make the voyage safely.
Waypoint: An intermediate turning or check point set in the passage plan.
Dümen Açısı: The angle by which the rudder is turned to port or starboard from the midships position.
Derinlik Ölçer (Echo Sounder): Equipment that measures the depth of water below the ship by sending sound pulses to the seabed.
Fener (Lighthouse): A light, fixed on the coast or at sea, that guides ships.
Şamandıra (Buoy): A floating mark moored on the sea surface to help safe navigation.
IALA İşaretleme Sistemi: The international rules for buoys and marks; divided into Region A and Region B.
Kıyı Seyri (Coastal Navigation): Navigation close to the coast using visual references and electronic aids.
Açık Deniz Seyri (Ocean Navigation): Navigation far from the coast using celestial bodies and electronic systems.
GPS: Global Positioning System; gives position, speed and time from satellite signals.
Gyro Pusula: A compass that uses the Earth's rotation to point to true north; mechanical or with optical (laser/fibre-optic) sensors.
Manyetik Pusula: The traditional compass, which points north according to the Earth's magnetic field.
Running Fix: A position found from two bearings of the same object taken at different times.
Cross Bearing: A position found from bearings of two or more objects taken at the same time.
Set & Drift: The effect of the current on the ship: set is the direction of the current, drift its speed.
Leeway: The sideways movement of the ship off her course caused by the wind.
GM (Metasentrik Yükseklik): The vertical distance between the centre of gravity G and the metacentre M; the main measure of initial stability.
Serbest Yüzey Etkisi: The loss of GM caused by liquid moving in partly filled tanks.
Ağırlık Merkezleri (KG): The vertical distance of the ship's centre of gravity above the keel; a critical value in stability calculations.
Trim: The fore-and-aft inclination of the ship; trim by the head or trim by the stern.
Deplasman (Displacement): The weight of water displaced by the ship; expressed in tonnes.
Yüzdürme Merkezi (B – Buoyancy): The geometric centre of the underwater volume of the hull.
GZ (Doğrultucu Kol): The horizontal distance between the centre of gravity and the line of action of buoyancy when the ship is heeled.
BM (Metasentrik Yarıçap): The distance between the centre of buoyancy B and the metacentre M; BM = I / ∇.
KB: The vertical distance from the keel to the centre of buoyancy.
KM: The vertical distance from the keel to the metacentre; KM = KB + BM.
KG: The vertical distance from the keel to the ship's centre of gravity.
Doğrultucu Moment: The moment that returns a heeled ship to the upright; M = Δ × GZ.
Devrilme Momenti: The moment of the external forces that heel the ship; caused by wind, waves or shifting cargo.
Denge Açısı (Angle of Loll): The angle of heel at which a ship with negative initial GM comes to rest.
Dinamik Stabilite: The area under the GZ curve; it shows the work needed to heel the ship.
Statik Stabilite Eğrisi (GZ Curve): A graph of GZ against the angle of heel; the basic tool of stability assessment.
TPC (Tonnes Per Centimetre): The weight that changes the mean draught by one centimetre.
MCT (Moment to Change Trim): The moment that changes the trim by one centimetre; used in trim calculations.
LCG (Longitudinal Centre of Gravity): The fore-and-aft position of the centre of gravity.
LCB (Longitudinal Centre of Buoyancy): The fore-and-aft position of the centre of buoyancy.
İnklinasyon Deneyi (Inclining Test): A test in which known weights are shifted across the deck to find the ship's KG.
Permeabilite: The proportion of a space that can be filled by water; used in damage stability calculations.
Floodable Length: The greatest length of a compartment that can be flooded without the ship sinking beyond the margin line.
Yük Kaydırma: Movement of cargo that moves the centre of gravity; it can cause a dangerous list.
Karina (Hull): The part of the hull below the waterline.
Su Çekimi (Draft): The vertical distance from the waterline to the bottom of the keel.
Fribord (Freeboard): The vertical distance from the waterline to the deck; enough freeboard is essential for seaworthiness.
Plimsoll Markası: The marks on the ship's side that show the maximum permitted draught for different seasons and waters.
Kavitasyon: The formation and collapse of vapour bubbles in a liquid when the pressure falls below the vapour pressure.
Dizel Motor (Marine Diesel): A compression-ignition internal combustion engine used as the main propulsion of most ships.
Turboşarj (Turbocharger): A unit driven by the exhaust gas that delivers compressed air to the cylinders; it increases engine power and efficiency.
SFOC (Specific Fuel Oil Consumption): The amount of fuel the engine burns per unit of power produced; expressed in g/kWh.
Separatör (Purifier): A centrifuge that removes water and solid particles from fuel oil and lubricating oil.
Yağlama Sistemi: The system that circulates oil to reduce friction between engine and machinery parts.
Soğutma Sistemi: The fresh water and sea water circuits that keep the main engine and auxiliary machinery from overheating.
Kazan (Boiler): A pressure vessel that heats water to produce steam for auxiliary machinery and heating.
Jeneratör: A machine that converts mechanical energy into electrical energy and supplies the ship's electrical load.
Şaft (Shaft): The shaft that transmits the rotation of the main engine to the propeller.
Pervane (Propeller): A bladed device that produces thrust as it turns and drives the ship ahead or astern.
Dümen (Rudder): The movable blade at the stern that is turned to change the ship's heading.
Bow Thruster: A propeller in a transverse tunnel in the bow; it improves manoeuvring at low speed.
Stern Tube: The tube through which the propeller shaft leaves the hull; it contains the shaft bearings and seals.
Yardımcı Motor: An engine on board used to generate electricity and drive auxiliary systems.
Emercensi Jeneratör: The generator that starts and supplies essential services when the main power supply fails.
Egzoz Gazı Temizleme (Scrubber): An emission control system that removes sulphur oxides from the exhaust gas by washing it.
Balast Pompası: The pump used to take sea water into and discharge it from the ballast tanks.
Sintine Pompası: The pump used to collect and pump out bilge water.
OWS (Oil Water Separator): Equipment that separates oil from bilge water so that it can be discharged within the legal limit of 15 ppm.
İncineratör (Yakma Fırını): A furnace that burns solid waste and oil sludge produced on board at high temperature.
Kompresör: A machine that produces compressed air for starting the engines and for pneumatic systems.
Piston: The engine part that moves up and down in the cylinder and converts gas pressure into mechanical work.
Silindir Gömleği (Cylinder Liner): The replaceable steel sleeve fitted in the cylinder block, in which the piston moves.
Süpap (Valve): A mechanical part that opens and closes the inlet and exhaust passages of the engine.
Dökme Yük (Bulk Cargo): Cargo such as grain, coal or ore loaded directly into the hold without packaging.
Konteyner: A standard-sized metal box (20 ft, 40 ft) used to carry cargo.
TEU (Twenty-foot Equivalent Unit): One 20 ft container equivalent; the standard unit for the capacity of ships and terminals.
Stowage Factor: The volume that one tonne of cargo occupies in the hold; expressed in m³/t.
Broken Stowage: The proportion of hold space that cannot be used because of the gaps between packages.
Dunnage: Timber, boards, mats or air bags used to protect cargo against moisture, damage and shifting.
Lashing: Securing cargo with lashings so that it cannot shift at sea.
Manifest: The document listing all the cargo carried on board.
Bill of Lading (Konşimento): A document issued by the carrier: a receipt for the cargo shipped, evidence of the contract of carriage and a document of title.
Ambar Kapağı (Hatch Cover): The steel cover that closes a hatch opening weathertight.
Grain Stability: The stability assessment of the risk that grain shifts at sea and causes a dangerous list.
IMDG Code: The International Maritime Dangerous Goods Code: the rules for carrying dangerous goods in packaged form by sea.
IMSBC Code: The IMO code for the safe carriage of solid bulk cargoes.
Draft Survey: A method of calculating the weight of cargo loaded or discharged from the ship's draught readings.
Ullage: The empty space in a tank, measured from the liquid surface to the top of the tank.
Sounding: The depth of liquid in a tank, measured from the bottom of the tank.
Deadweight (DWT): The total weight the ship can carry: cargo, fuel, water, stores and crew.
Lightweight: The weight of the ship itself, without cargo, fuel, water and stores.
Tonnage (Gross / Net): Measures of the ship's internal volume: gross tonnage covers the whole ship, net tonnage the cargo-carrying spaces.
Reefer Konteyner: A container with its own refrigeration unit for temperature-controlled cargo.
Tanker: A ship designed to carry liquid cargo in bulk (oil, chemicals, LPG/LNG).
RoRo (Roll-on Roll-off): A ship on which vehicles and wheeled cargo are driven on and off over a ramp.
SOLAS: The International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea; it sets standards for the construction, equipment and operation of ships.
MARPOL: The International Convention for the Prevention of Pollution from Ships.
ISM Code: The International Safety Management Code; the standard for safety management in ship operation.
ISPS Code: The International Ship and Port Facility Security Code; measures against security threats such as terrorism.
Can Yeleği (Life Jacket): Personal equipment that keeps a person afloat in the water; required for every person on board.
Can Simidi (Life Buoy): A ring-shaped buoyant device thrown to a person in the water.
Filika (Lifeboat): An enclosed boat used to evacuate the crew and passengers when the ship is abandoned.
Can Salı (Life Raft): An inflatable survival craft; inflated automatically or by hand.
EPIRB: Emergency Position-Indicating Radio Beacon; transmits a distress alert via satellite.
SART: Search and Rescue Transponder; shows its position on the radar screens of searching ships and aircraft.
GMDSS: Global Maritime Distress and Safety System; the international system for distress and safety communications.
MOB (Man Overboard): The emergency when a person falls into the sea; the recovery manoeuvre and procedure are started at once.
Muster Station: The place where the crew and passengers assemble in an emergency.
Fire Drill: A practical exercise in which the crew practise firefighting procedures.
Abandon Ship Drill: A drill covering mustering and the use of lifeboats and liferafts.
SCBA: Self-Contained Breathing Apparatus; used for entering enclosed spaces and for firefighting.
CO₂ Söndürme Sistemi: A fixed carbon dioxide system used to extinguish fires in the engine room and cargo spaces.
Köpüklü Söndürme: A foam-based system used on fires in flammable liquids.
Yangın Tulumbası (Fire Pump): A pump that supplies water under pressure to the fire main and hoses; there are main and emergency fire pumps.
Emercensi Dümen: The arrangement used to steer the ship when the main steering system fails.
SOPEP: Shipboard Oil Pollution Emergency Plan; the procedures to follow after an oil spill.
Enclosed Space Entry: The procedure for entering an enclosed space; it requires atmosphere testing, ventilation and supervision.
Hot Work Permit: A written permit required before hot work such as welding or cutting.
Buharlaşma (Evaporation): The change of water from liquid to gas as it absorbs heat; it affects humidity and the weather.
Dew Point (Çiy Noktası): The temperature to which air must be cooled to become saturated, so that condensation begins.
Beaufort Skalası: The international scale that grades wind force from 0 to 12.
Tropikal Siklon: A rotating storm that forms over warm seas, with violent winds and heavy rain.
Kasırga (Hurricane): A tropical cyclone with winds of 64 knots or more in the Atlantic and the North-East Pacific.
Tayfun (Typhoon): A tropical cyclone of hurricane strength in the North-West Pacific.
Barometrik Basınç: The weight of the atmosphere at a given point; measured in hPa (mbar).
Antisiklon (High Pressure): A centre of high pressure; it usually brings settled, fair weather.
Siklon (Low Pressure): A centre of low pressure; associated with wind, rain and storms.
Cephe (Front): The boundary zone where air masses of different temperature and humidity meet.
Sis (Fog): Condensation of water vapour near the surface that reduces visibility to less than 1000 metres.
Deniz Suyu Sıcaklığı (SST): The temperature of the sea surface; important for weather forecasting and the development of tropical cyclones.
Trade Winds (Alize Rüzgârları): The steady north-easterly and south-easterly winds of the tropics.
Gel-Git (Tide): The periodic rise and fall of sea level caused by the attraction of the Moon and the Sun.
Spring Tide (Büyük Gel-Git): The tide with the greatest range, at new moon and full moon, when the pull of the Sun and the Moon combine.
Neap Tide (Küçük Gel-Git): The tide with the smallest range, at first and last quarter, when the Sun and the Moon pull at right angles.
Swell (Ölü Deniz): Long-period waves that have travelled away from the area where they were generated and become regular.
Navtex: A system that automatically receives navigational and meteorological warnings in printed or displayed text.
Rüzgâr Gülü: A diagram showing how often the wind blows from each direction, and how strongly, at a given place.
İzobar: A line on a weather chart joining places of equal pressure.
Dalga Yükü (Wave Load): The dynamic loads caused by waves on the hull; used in seakeeping and strength calculations.
Direnç (Resistance): The total force that opposes the ship's motion through the water; mainly frictional and wave-making resistance.
Sürtünme Direnci (Frictional Resistance): The part of the resistance caused by friction between the hull and the water.
Dalga Direnci (Wave Resistance): The part of the resistance caused by the energy spent in creating the ship's wave system.
Froude Sayısı: A dimensionless number relating ship speed to wave making; Fn = V / √(g × L).
Reynolds Sayısı: A dimensionless number that characterises the flow; it separates laminar from turbulent flow.
İtme Kuvveti (Thrust): The force produced by the turning propeller that drives the ship.
Wake Fraction: The proportional difference between the ship's speed and the speed of the water flowing into the propeller.
Thrust Deduction: The fraction of propeller thrust lost because the working propeller increases the hull resistance.
Propulsive Efficiency: How efficiently engine power is turned into effective power to move the ship; the product of hull, propeller and other efficiencies.
Squat Effect: The sinkage and change of trim of a ship moving in shallow water, increasing with speed; full-bodied ships (high Cb) squat more at the bow, fine-lined ships at the stern.
Bank Effect: In a narrow channel, the nearby bank draws the stern towards it and pushes the bow away.
Slamming: The violent impact of the bow on the sea surface in waves; it causes high structural stresses.
Broaching: In a following sea, the ship swings uncontrollably broadside to the waves; it carries a risk of capsizing.
Parametrik Rolling: Large, rapidly growing rolling caused when the wave encounter period is about half the ship's natural roll period.
Added Mass: The extra mass effect of the water that has to be accelerated with the ship when its speed or motion changes.
Sinkage & Trim: The bodily sinkage and change of trim of a moving ship, which increase with speed in shallow water.
Boundary Layer: The thin layer of water next to the hull in which the flow speed changes from zero to the free-stream speed.
Ana Şalt (Main Switchboard): The central board through which the power from the generators is distributed.
Shore Connection: Connecting the ship to the shore electricity supply in port, so that the generators can be stopped.
UPS: Uninterruptible Power Supply; keeps critical equipment running during a power failure.
VHF Telsiz: A very high frequency radio used for short-range maritime communication.
MF/HF Telsiz: A radio used for medium and long-range maritime communication.
Inmarsat: The satellite system that provides voice, data and distress communications for ships.
Log (Hız Ölçer): An instrument that measures the ship's speed through the water or over the ground.
Anemometre: An instrument that measures wind speed and direction.
Voyage Data Recorder (VDR): Equipment that records navigation, machinery and bridge data; the ship's 'black box'.
Autopilot: An electronic steering control system that keeps the ship on the set course automatically.
COLREG: The International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea; the rules ships follow when they meet.
STCW: The International Convention on Standards of Training, Certification and Watchkeeping for Seafarers.
MLC 2006: The Maritime Labour Convention; it sets the working and living conditions of seafarers.
Flag State (Bayrak Devleti): The state in which the ship is registered; it is responsible for the ship's technical and safety supervision.
Port State Control (PSC): Inspection of foreign ships in port to check that they comply with international standards.
Class Survey (Klas Denetimi): A periodic survey by the classification society to check the ship's structure and machinery.
P&I Club: A mutual insurance association that covers shipowners' third-party liabilities.
Charter Party: The contract for hiring a ship; arranged as a voyage, time or bareboat charter.
Salvage (Kurtarma): Saving a ship or cargo in danger; successful salvage gives a right to a salvage award.
General Average (Müşterek Avarya): The principle that sacrifices and expenses made to save the ship and cargo from a common danger are shared by all parties.
Demurrage: The agreed amount paid when the ship is kept for loading or discharging beyond the allowed laytime.
Despatch: The amount earned when loading or discharging is completed before the laytime has expired.
NOR (Notice of Readiness): The written notice that the ship is ready to load or discharge.
Lay Time (Starya Süresi): The time allowed for loading and discharging.
LOF (Lloyd's Open Form): The standard salvage agreement, based on the principle 'no cure, no pay'.
Yanaşma (Berthing): Bringing the ship alongside a quay or pier under control and making her fast.
Kalkma (Unberthing): Letting go from the berth and getting under way.
Demir Atma (Anchoring): Letting go the anchor to the seabed so that the ship stays in position.
Demir Alma (Weighing Anchor): Heaving the anchor up from the seabed to end the anchoring.
Römorkör (Tug): A small, powerful vessel that helps large ships manoeuvre in harbour.
Kılavuz Kaptan (Pilot): A person with local knowledge who boards to advise the master on the bridge when the ship enters or leaves port.
Pilot Merdiveni: A rope ladder rigged over the ship's side for the pilot to board.
Çıpa (Anchor): The heavy fitting that holds the ship in position by gripping the seabed; types include Hall, AC-14 and Danforth.
Zincir (Chain): The heavy steel chain that connects the anchor to the ship; its length is measured in shackles.
Posa (Shackle): The unit of length of anchor cable; one shackle is 27.5 metres (15 fathoms).
Usturmaça (Fender): A cushion placed between the ship and the quay to absorb the impact.
Swing Circle: The circle in which an anchored ship can swing with wind and current; it decides the safe anchoring distance.
Turning Circle: The circle the ship makes when turning with full (hard over) rudder; a measure of manoeuvrability.
Advance & Transfer: The distances the ship moves ahead (advance) and sideways (transfer) after the rudder is put over.
Crash Stop: In an emergency, stopping the ship by going from full ahead to full astern.
Dead Slow: The lowest engine speed order; used during manoeuvring.
VTS (Vessel Traffic Service): A shore-based service that monitors and organises ship traffic in ports and narrow waters.
Kanal Seyrüseferi: Passing through man-made waterways such as Suez and Panama; it involves special rules and pilotage.
Dry Dock (Havuz): A dock from which the water is pumped out so that the ship's underwater hull can be maintained and repaired.
Şamandıraya Bağlanma: Making the ship fast to a fixed mooring buoy with ropes instead of anchoring.
Amade: The ship is ready to sail; all checks have been completed and she is ready to depart.
Demir Yeri (Anchorage): A designated area with suitable depth and seabed for anchoring.
Enine Perde (Bulkhead): A vertical structural division that splits the hull into watertight compartments.
Forkastel (Forecastle): The raised part of the deck at the bow; it carries the anchoring and mooring equipment.
Güverte Ambarı (Tweendeck): An intermediate deck between the lower hold and the upper deck; used for general cargo.
Havuzlama (Dry Docking): Taking the ship into dry dock to maintain and repair the underwater hull.
Koferdamı (Cofferdam): A narrow empty space between two tanks or compartments, provided to prevent leakage from one to the other.
Lumboz (Porthole): A round window in the ship's side that gives light and ventilation.
Manika: The opening of a ventilation trunk on deck; mushroom or gooseneck shaped.
Mayıstra: The largest sail, set on the mainmast; the main driving sail of a sailing ship.
Neta: Order and tidiness on deck; making all loose gear secure.
Orsalamak: To turn a sailing vessel's head towards the wind.
Pupa: The after end of the ship; a wind from the stern blows from right astern (a following wind).
Safra (Ballast): Sea water or solid weight carried in tanks to give the ship the required stability, draught and trim.
Uskuna (Schooner): A sailing vessel with two or more masts and fore-and-aft sails.
Mercator Projeksiyonu: A cylindrical chart projection on which rhumb lines are straight lines; areas are increasingly enlarged towards high latitudes.
Gnomonic Projeksiyon: A chart projection on which great circles are straight lines; used for planning great circle sailing.
Dead Reckoning (Tahmini Seyir): Working out the ship's position from the last known position using course and speed through the water only.
Fix (Kesin Mevki): A reliable position found by observation or electronic aids.
Estimated Position (EP): A position estimated from dead reckoning with corrections for current and wind; less reliable than a fix.
DLat (Enlem Değişimi): The difference in latitude between two positions; expressed in minutes of arc.
DLong (Boylam Değişimi): The difference in longitude between two positions; expressed in minutes of arc.
Departure: The east-west distance in nautical miles that corresponds to a difference of longitude; Dep = D.Long × cos(Lat).
Vertex (Tepe Noktası): The point on a great circle nearest to the pole; there the track reaches its highest latitude.
Composite Great Circle: A route that follows great circles and a parallel of latitude so as not to go beyond a limiting latitude.
Course Made Good (CMG): The direction actually made good by the ship, including the effects of current and wind.
Speed Made Good (SMG): The speed actually made good over the ground, including the effect of current.
Chart Datum: The reference level from which charted depths are measured; usually Lowest Astronomical Tide (LAT).
Sextant: An optical instrument that measures the angle between a celestial body and the horizon; used in celestial navigation.
Chronometer: A precise clock that keeps Greenwich time; essential for finding longitude.
Nautical Almanac: The annual publication giving the daily positions (GHA, Dec) of the celestial bodies.
Sight Reduction Tables: Pre-computed tables used to solve celestial navigation sights.
Height of Eye: The height of the observer's eye above the sea surface; used in sextant altitude corrections.
Dip (Ufuk Alçalması): The angle between the true horizontal and the visible horizon, caused by the observer's height of eye.
Index Error: The sextant error that exists when the index and horizon mirrors are not parallel at zero.
Azimut: The horizontal direction of a celestial body or object, measured clockwise from north.
Amplitude: The angle between true east or west and the direction of the Sun or another body at its rising or setting.
Intercept (Aradaki Fark): The difference between the observed and calculated altitudes; used to draw the position line.
Position Line (Mevki Doğrusu): A line, obtained from an observation, on which the ship is somewhere; two position lines that cross give a fix.
Under Keel Clearance (UKC): The safe depth of water between the bottom of the keel and the seabed.
Traffic Separation Scheme (TSS): A routeing measure that separates opposing streams of traffic into lanes.
Precautionary Area: A defined area where ships must navigate with particular caution; often where traffic lanes meet.
Tidal Stream: The horizontal movement of water caused by the tide; its direction and rate change through the tidal cycle.
Chart Correction: Updating nautical charts with the information published in Notices to Mariners.
Notice to Mariners (NtM): Periodic notices published to keep charts and nautical publications up to date.
Metacenter (M): At small angles of heel, the point where the line of action of buoyancy crosses the ship's centreline.
Vanishing Angle: The angle of heel at which GZ returns to zero; beyond it the ship has no righting lever.
Range of Stability: The range of heel over which GZ stays positive; a wide range means a large safety margin.
Righting Lever Maximum: The largest value on the GZ curve, where the ship's resistance to heeling is greatest.
Cross Curves of Stability: Curves showing KN at fixed angles of heel for different displacements.
Intact Stability: The stability of the undamaged ship; it must meet the minimum criteria set by IMO.
Damage Stability: The stability of the ship with one or more compartments flooded.
Subdivision: Dividing the hull into compartments by watertight bulkheads; it protects the ship against sinking.
Margin Line: A line 76 mm below the upper surface of the bulkhead deck at the side; in damage calculations the waterline must not go above it.
Heel (Yatma): A transverse inclination of the ship caused by an external force such as wind, a shifted weight or turning.
List: A transverse inclination that stays because of internal causes, such as off-centre cargo or tank contents.
Loll: The state of a ship with negative initial GM that lies at an angle of loll; an extremely dangerous condition.
Waterplane Area: The area enclosed by the waterline; used in TPC and BM calculations.
Block Coefficient (Cb): A measure of the fullness of the hull: the underwater volume divided by length × breadth × draught.
Midship Coefficient (Cm): The ratio of the immersed midship section area to breadth × draught.
Prismatic Coefficient (Cp): The ratio of the underwater volume to midship section area × length; it affects resistance and speed.
Crosshead (Çapraz Kafa): In two-stroke low-speed engines, the sliding joint that connects the piston rod to the connecting rod.
Crankshaft (Krank Mili): The main engine shaft that converts the reciprocating motion of the pistons into rotation.
Camshaft (Kam Mili): The shaft whose cams control the timing of the valves and fuel pumps.
Connecting Rod (Biyel Kolu): The rod that connects the piston (or crosshead) to the crankshaft and converts reciprocating motion into rotation.
Fuel Injector (Enjektör): The device that sprays atomised fuel into the cylinder at high pressure.
Exhaust Valve (Egzoz Süpabı): The valve that lets the burnt gases out of the cylinder.
Scavenging (Süpürme): Removing the burnt gases from the cylinder and filling it with fresh air.
Deaerator: Equipment that removes dissolved oxygen and gases from the boiler feed water to prevent corrosion.
Economizer: A heat exchanger that uses exhaust gas heat to preheat boiler feed water or raise steam.
Evaporator (Tatlı Su Üreteci): Equipment that produces fresh water by evaporating sea water, usually with engine waste heat or low-pressure steam.
Oily Water Separator (OWS): The separator that reduces the oil content of bilge water below 15 ppm so that it can be discharged legally.
Sewage Treatment Plant: The system that treats the ship's sewage biologically or chemically before discharge.
Ballast Water Treatment (BWTS): A system that kills or removes organisms and pathogens in ballast water to prevent their spread.
Stern Tube Seal: The seal that keeps water out where the propeller shaft passes through the hull.
Controllable Pitch Propeller (CPP): A propeller whose blade angle can be changed; thrust is adjusted while engine speed stays constant.
Fixed Pitch Propeller (FPP): The traditional propeller with fixed blades; thrust is controlled by the engine speed and direction.
Reduction Gear (Dişli Kutusu): A gearbox that reduces the speed of a high-speed engine to the speed the propeller needs.
Heat Exchanger (Isı Değiştirici): Equipment that transfers heat between two fluids; used in cooling and heating circuits.
Centrifugal Pump: A pump with a rotating impeller that moves liquid by centrifugal force; common for cooling and ballast.
Positive Displacement Pump: A pump that moves a fixed volume of liquid each stroke or revolution; used for lubricating oil and fuel transfer.
Air Compressor (Hava Kompresörü): A compressor that produces compressed air at about 30 bar for starting the main engine and for control systems.
Indicator Diagram: A pressure-volume diagram of the cylinder; used for performance analysis and fault finding.
Mean Effective Pressure (MEP): The average effective pressure in the cylinder over one cycle; used to calculate engine power.
Brake Power: The power measured at the engine output shaft; expressed in kW.
Indicated Power: The power developed in the cylinders, calculated from the gas pressure; mechanical losses are not deducted.
Thermal Efficiency: The proportion of the fuel's heat energy that is turned into mechanical work; expressed as a percentage.
LSA Code: The International Life-Saving Appliance Code; standards for lifeboats, liferafts, lifejackets and other life-saving appliances.
FSS Code: The International Code for Fire Safety Systems; standards for fire detection and extinguishing systems.
IAMSAR Manual: The International Aeronautical and Maritime Search and Rescue Manual; it sets out the procedures for SAR operations.
Williamson Turn: A man overboard recovery manoeuvre that brings the ship back onto her own track, in the opposite direction.
Scharnow Turn: A man overboard manoeuvre used when the person has been missing for some time (delayed action).
Anderson Turn: A quick, single-turn man overboard manoeuvre for ships with a tight turning circle (immediate action).
Immersion Suit: A waterproof, insulated full-body suit that protects the wearer in cold water.
Thermal Protective Aid (TPA): A bag or suit of waterproof material that reduces body heat loss in a liferaft or lifeboat.
Pyrotechnic Signals: Distress signals such as rocket parachute flares, hand flares and buoyant smoke signals.
EEBD (Emergency Escape Breathing Device): A portable breathing device that gives a short supply of air for escaping from a dangerous atmosphere.
Fixed Fire Detection System: Fixed fire detection and fire alarm system
A fixed system that detects fire with smoke, heat or flame detectors and raises the alarm.
Sprinkler System: A water spray system that operates automatically when heat opens the sprinkler heads; required on passenger ships.
Inert Gas System (IGS): A system that fills the cargo tanks of tankers with gas of low oxygen content to prevent explosions.
Permit to Work: A written permit issued before hazardous work such as hot work, enclosed space entry or work at height.
Risk Assessment: A systematic review that identifies the hazards of a job and plans the control measures.
Toolbox Meeting: A short safety briefing before work, in which the hazards and precautions are explained to the team.
Near Miss Report: A report of an event that could have caused an accident; important for building a safety culture.
Yoğunlaşma (Condensation): The change of water vapour into liquid as it cools; the process behind cloud, fog and dew.
Adveksiyon Sisi: Fog that forms when warm, moist air moves over a colder sea surface.
Radyasyon Sisi: Fog that forms over land at night when the ground cools and the air above it reaches its dew point.
Coriolis Kuvveti: The apparent force caused by the Earth's rotation; it deflects winds and currents to the right in the northern hemisphere and to the left in the southern.
Geostrofik Rüzgâr: The theoretical wind blowing parallel to the isobars when the pressure gradient force and the Coriolis force balance.
Konveksiyon: Vertical air movement as heated air rises and cools; it produces cumulus clouds and showers.
Soğuk Cephe: The boundary where a cold air mass pushes under a warm air mass and lifts it.
Sıcak Cephe: The boundary where a warm air mass rises slowly over a cold air mass.
Oklüzyon Cephesi: A front formed when the cold front overtakes the warm front and lifts the warm air off the surface.
Hava Kütlesi: A large body of air with similar temperature and humidity over a wide area.
Jet Stream: A narrow band of very strong wind near the tropopause; it can reach 200-300 knots.
ITCZ (Ekvatoral Konverjans): The tropical belt where the trade winds of the two hemispheres meet; an area of heavy rain and thunderstorms.
Fetch: The distance of open sea over which the wind blows unobstructed; it directly affects the size of the waves.
Significant Wave Height (Hs): The average height of the highest one third of the waves; the main measure of sea state.
Typhoon Signal: A warning signal that announces the approach of a tropical cyclone.
Buys Ballot Kuralı: In the northern hemisphere, if you stand with your back to the wind, the low pressure is on your left.
Squall (Bora): A sudden, short-lived strong increase in wind; often with heavy rain and poor visibility.
Waterspout (Hortum): A rotating column of wind over the sea, hanging from a cumulonimbus cloud and drawing up spray.
Bulbous Bow (Bodoslama Bülbü): A bulb projecting forward below the waterline at the bow; it reduces wave-making resistance and saves fuel.
Bilge Keel: A fin fitted along the turn of the bilge to damp rolling.
Stabilizer Fin: An active fin projecting from the ship's side that automatically reduces rolling at sea.
Slip (Kayma): The difference between the theoretical and the actual advance of the propeller; expressed as a percentage.
Pitch (Hatve): The distance a propeller would theoretically advance in one revolution.
Cavitation: Vapour bubbles that form on the propeller blades where the pressure drops and then collapse; it causes erosion and loss of efficiency.
Interaction Effect: The hydrodynamic forces between two ships passing close to each other.
Shallow Water Effect: In shallow water the flow under the ship speeds up and the pressure drops; the ship sinks and steers less well.
Trim Optimization: Choosing the trim at which the ship has the least resistance; it saves fuel.
Alternator: A generator that produces alternating current; on ships usually 440 V 60 Hz or 380 V 50 Hz.
Transformer: An electromagnetic device that raises or lowers AC voltage.
Circuit Breaker (Şalter): A protective switch that opens the circuit automatically on overcurrent or short circuit.
Frequency Converter: Electronic equipment that converts frequency and voltage, for example for a shore power connection.
Synchroscope: An instrument that shows whether the frequency and phase of an incoming generator match the busbar, before paralleling.
AVR (Automatic Voltage Regulator): The circuit that keeps the generator output voltage constant.
Earth Fault Monitor: An instrument that detects earth faults in an insulated (unearthed) distribution system.
Motor Starter: The circuit that starts an electric motor under control by limiting the starting current.
PLC (Programmable Logic Controller): A programmable controller used for machinery and process control in shipboard automation.
SCADA: Software for central monitoring and control of the engine room and auxiliary systems.
BWM Convention: The Ballast Water Management Convention; it aims to stop the spread of organisms in ships' ballast water.
SEEMP: Ship Energy Efficiency Management Plan; the mandatory plan for operational energy efficiency measures.
EEDI: Energy Efficiency Design Index; the mandatory design standard for the CO₂ efficiency of new ships.
CII Rating: Carbon Intensity Indicator; rates a ship's annual operational carbon efficiency from A to E.
DOC (Document of Compliance): The ISM Code certificate showing that the company's safety management system complies.
SMC (Safety Management Certificate): The ISM Code certificate issued to the ship, showing that its safety management system complies.
IOPP Certificate: The International Oil Pollution Prevention Certificate, issued under MARPOL Annex I.
Load Line Certificate: The certificate confirming the ship's assigned load lines and freeboards.
Safety Equipment Certificate: The certificate showing that the life-saving and fire safety equipment complies with SOLAS.
Tonnage Certificate: The certificate stating the ship's gross and net tonnage.
Grain Loading Diagram: A diagram showing the effect of grain cargo on stability for different hold fillings.
Lashing Calculator: A tool for calculating the forces on container and cargo lashings.
Cargo Securing Manual (CSM): The mandatory ship-specific manual on cargo securing procedures and securing equipment.
Ventilation Hold: Ventilating the holds to control humidity and temperature; it prevents sweat and condensation.
Sweat (Terleme): Condensation on the cargo or on the hold structure caused by temperature differences; divided into cargo sweat and ship's sweat.
TML (Transportable Moisture Limit): The maximum moisture content at which a solid bulk cargo that may liquefy can be carried safely.
Flow Moisture Point (FMP): The moisture content at which a solid bulk cargo begins to behave like a liquid; TML = 0.9 × FMP.
Liquefaction: A solid bulk cargo starting to behave like a liquid under vibration and ship motion; it can lead to loss of stability and capsizing.
Fumigation: Killing insects and pests in the cargo with a toxic gas.
Classification Survey: A technical inspection by the classification society of the ship's structure and equipment at set intervals.
Damage Report (Hasar Raporu): A written record of damage or shortages found in the cargo.
Letter of Protest: A formal letter objecting to cargo damage, delay or unsuitable conditions.
Dangerous Goods Declaration: The document in which the shipper declares the class, properties and emergency information of dangerous goods.
Mediterranean Mooring: Mooring stern-to the quay with the bow held by the anchors; common in the Mediterranean.
Single Point Mooring (SPM): A buoy offshore to which a tanker moors at one point while loading or discharging.
Parallel Body: The midship length of the hull over which the cross-section stays the same.
Pivot Point: The point about which the ship appears to turn; when going ahead it lies well forward.
Tactical Diameter: The distance the ship has moved sideways from her original track when she has turned through 180° with hard over rudder.
Kick (Başlangıç Sapması): Right after the rudder is put over, the stern swings away from the direction of the turn and the ship moves briefly sideways in the opposite direction.
Transverse Thrust: The sideways push of the propeller on the stern; it governs handling at low speed.
Approach Speed: The ship's sideways speed towards the berth while coming alongside; it must not exceed what the fenders can absorb.
STS Operation: Ship-to-ship transfer: two ships lie alongside each other to transfer cargo.
Alabora: A ship or boat turning completely over, so that the keel comes above the water.
Arma: On sailing ships, the whole arrangement of masts, yards, shrouds, stays and ropes.
Ayna Kıç: A stern with a flat, vertical end; widely used on modern cargo ships.
Demir Taramak: The anchor fails to hold and drags along the seabed; caused by poor holding ground or too little cable.
Duba: A flat-bottomed floating platform, with or without its own engine; used for cargo transfer, as a landing stage or as a working platform.
Gemiadamı: A person employed on board a ship in any capacity; includes the master, officers and ratings.
Iskarmoz: On small boats, the pin or fork on the gunwale that the oar rests against when rowing.
Kontra: Putting the rudder to the opposite side to check the ship's swing.
Tayfa: A crew member of the deck or engine department who is not an officer.
Kazık Bağı (Clove Hitch): A hitch used to make a rope fast to a post or bollard; quick to tie and to untie.
Gemici Bağı (Bowline): A knot that forms a fixed loop at the end of a rope which does not slip or tighten; the most basic seaman's knot.
Yoma (Sheet Bend): A knot used to join two ropes, also of different thickness.
Balıkçı Bağı (Fisherman's Knot): A strong knot used to join two lines permanently.
Figure of Eight: A stopper knot that prevents the end of a rope from running out through a block or a hole.
Constrictor Bağı: A hitch that grips a round object very tightly; used, for example, to secure a hose.
Rolling Hitch: A friction hitch tied to a rope or spar that holds against a pull along it; used to take the strain off a rope under load.
Kısa Ek (Short Splice): Joining two rope ends permanently by interweaving their strands; it increases the diameter of the rope.
Uzun Ek (Long Splice): A splice that joins two ropes without increasing the diameter; used where the rope must run through a block.
Koçboynuzu: A metal fitting with two horns around which a rope is made fast.
Panama Chock: A closed fairlead at the ship's side through which mooring lines are led; required for the Panama Canal transit.
Çıma Halatı (Heaving Line): A light line with a weighted end, thrown ashore or to another vessel to pass the mooring lines.
Sentetik Halat: Rope made of man-made fibres such as nylon, polyester, polypropylene or HMPE.
Tel Halat (Wire Rope): High-strength rope made of steel wires; used for cranes, derricks and cargo securing.
SWL (Safe Working Load): The maximum load that a rope, chain or item of lifting gear may lift or hold in normal use.
MBL (Minimum Breaking Load): The smallest force at which a new rope or chain is guaranteed not to break; the safety factor is MBL divided by SWL.
Snap Back Zone: The dangerous area into which a mooring line under tension can whip back if it parts.
Doubling the Angle: Doubling the angle on the bow
Finding the distance off an object by noting when its relative bearing doubles; the distance run between the two bearings equals the distance off.
Four Point Bearing: Finding the distance off an object from bearings at 45° and 90° on the bow; the distance run equals the distance off abeam.
Special Mark (Özel İşaret): In the IALA system, a yellow mark that shows a special area or feature, such as a cable area or firing range.
Cardinal Mark: In the IALA system, a mark placed north, east, south or west of a danger; it shows on which side the safe water lies.
Isolated Danger Mark: In the IALA system, a mark placed on a danger of limited size that has navigable water all around it.
Safe Water Mark: In the IALA system, a red and white vertically striped mark showing safe water all around; used as a landfall or mid-channel mark.
Liman Yanaşma Feneri: Lights at a harbour entrance that, when seen in line, mark the centre of a channel or the safe approach line.
Racon: A radar transponder that answers a radar pulse and shows a coded mark on the radar screen.
Radar Shadow: The blind area behind large objects that the radar beam cannot reach.
Lubber Line: The fixed line on the compass bowl or radar display that marks the ship's head.
Pelorus: A sighting device used to take bearings; it has no magnetic compass of its own.
Rate of Turn Indicator: An instrument showing how fast the ship is turning, in degrees per minute; required by SOLAS on ships of 50,000 GT and above.
Speed Log: An instrument that measures the ship's speed through the water or over the ground; Doppler or electromagnetic.
Parallel Indexing: A radar technique: lines drawn parallel to the planned track at a set distance from a fixed target are used to monitor the ship's position.
Stiff Ship (Sert Gemi): A ship with a large GM; she rolls quickly and violently and is uncomfortable, although her initial stability is high.
Tender Ship (Yumuşak Gemi): A ship with a small GM; she rolls slowly with a long period, and the risk of capsizing is higher.
Hogging: The middle of the ship bends upwards and the ends droop; it causes structural stress.
Sagging: The middle of the ship bends downwards and the ends rise; the opposite of hogging.
Still Water Bending Moment: The longitudinal bending moment caused by the distribution of weight and buoyancy in calm water; the basis of strength calculations.
Wave Bending Moment: The additional bending moment acting on the hull as waves pass.
Torsional Stress: Stress caused by twisting loads on the hull; especially critical on large container ships.
FWA (Fresh Water Allowance): The amount by which the draught increases when the ship passes from salt water into fresh water; expressed in mm.
DWA (Dock Water Allowance): The draught correction for the density of dock water between fresh and salt water.
Displacement Table: A hydrostatic table giving the ship's displacement at different draughts.
Hydrostatic Curves: Curves giving values such as TPC, MCTC, LCB and LCF against draught.
KN Curves: Cross curves of stability: KN plotted against displacement for fixed angles of heel.
Wall-Sided Formula: GZ = sin θ × (GM + ½ BM tan² θ); gives GZ for a wall-sided ship, valid until the deck edge immerses or the bilge emerges.
Bilge Radius: The radius of the curved plating where the ship's bottom turns into the side.
Shifting Boards: Vertical longitudinal divisions fitted in the holds to stop grain cargo from shifting.
Grain Heeling Moment: The heeling moment caused by an assumed shift of grain cargo; limited by the IMO Grain Code.
Blowdown: The controlled discharge of boiler water to reduce the dissolved solids in it.
Cylinder Lubrication: In two-stroke engines, the separate system that lubricates the cylinder liner and the piston rings.
Crankcase Explosion: A dangerous explosion caused when oil mist in the crankcase is ignited by a hot spot.
Oil Mist Detector (OMD): A detector that monitors the oil mist concentration in the crankcase and gives a warning before an explosion can occur.
Scavenge Fire: A fire in the scavenge air space caused by the ignition of oil and carbon deposits.
Stuffing Box: A packed gland that seals where a shaft or a rod passes through a casing or bulkhead.
Governor (Regülatör): The device that adjusts the fuel supply automatically to keep the engine speed constant as the load changes.
Indicator Card: The pressure-volume diagram taken from a cylinder; used to assess engine performance and find faults.
Compression Ratio: The cylinder volume with the piston at bottom dead centre divided by the volume at top dead centre.
Clearance Volume: The volume left in the cylinder when the piston is at top dead centre.
TDC (Top Dead Centre): The highest position of the piston in the cylinder.
BDC (Bottom Dead Centre): The lowest position of the piston in the cylinder.
Lub Oil Crosshead: The lubrication supply to the crosshead bearings; it needs oil at high pressure.
Plate Cooler: A plate-type heat exchanger; it transfers heat between sea water and fresh water.
Relief Valve: A safety valve that opens automatically on excess pressure to protect the system.
Thermostat: An automatic control element that keeps the cooling water temperature within a set range.
Jacket Water: The fresh water cooling circuit around the engine cylinders; a closed circuit.
Expansion Tank: The header tank of the cooling water circuit; it takes up the expansion of the water as it heats and lets air escape.
Sea Chest: A recess in the underwater hull, covered by a grating, through which sea water is drawn in.
Zinc Anode (Kurban Anot): A zinc anode fitted to the underwater hull that corrodes in place of the steel and prevents galvanic corrosion.
ICCP: An active system that protects the hull against corrosion with a current supplied from an external source.
Tank Top: The top plating of the double bottom; it forms the floor of the hold and carries the cargo weight.
Tweendeck: An intermediate deck between the lower hold and the upper deck; gives extra stowage space for general cargo.
Feeder Vessel: A small container ship that carries containers between smaller ports and the hub ports served by large ships.
FCL (Full Container Load): A container whose whole contents belong to one shipper.
LCL (Less than Container Load): A container filled with the goods of several shippers.
Outturn Report: A tally and condition report of the cargo after discharge.
Bagging: Putting bulk cargo into bags for carriage.
Ship's Figures: The cargo quantity found by the ship from a draught survey; compared with the shore figures.
Shore Figures: The cargo quantity found by the shore scales; a difference from the ship's figures can lead to a dispute.
Loading Computer: An onboard computer system that calculates the loading condition, stability and longitudinal strength.
COW (Crude Oil Washing): Washing the cargo tanks of a crude oil tanker with the crude oil cargo itself; required by MARPOL.
Inert Gas (Asal Gaz): Gas with a low oxygen content; used in the cargo tanks of tankers to prevent explosions.
Cargo Plan (Yükleme Planı): The plan showing where each part of the cargo is stowed; prepared with regard to stability and the order of ports.
Bay Plan: On container ships, the detailed plan showing the stowage position of every container in each bay.
Segregation: Keeping incompatible classes of dangerous goods apart by the required distances.
DSC (Digital Selective Calling): A system on VHF, MF and HF radios for sending automatic distress alerts and calling stations.
Inmarsat-C: A message-based satellite communication terminal; used for distress alerts and for receiving maritime safety information.
LRIT: Long-Range Identification and Tracking; ships' positions are reported to and followed by their flag states.
SSAS: Ship Security Alert System; sends a covert alert ashore in a security threat such as piracy.
Foam Monitor: A fixed or portable foam/water cannon on deck with a long throw.
Quick-Closing Valve: A valve on a fuel or oil tank that can be closed from a remote position in a fire.
Fire Damper: A flap in a ventilation duct that closes to stop fire spreading through the duct.
Watertight Door: A door in a watertight bulkhead; it can be closed locally or from a remote position.
Muster List: The official list of the duties and stations of every person on board in an emergency.
Emergency Towing Arrangement: The towing equipment kept ready at the bow and stern so that the ship can be towed in an emergency.
Lifeboat Releasing Gear: The mechanism that releases the lifeboat from the davit falls; on-load and off-load types exist.
Free-Fall Lifeboat: An enclosed lifeboat launched by sliding down a ramp at the stern and falling freely into the sea.
Rescue Boat: A fast boat used to recover persons from the water and to marshal liferafts.
Line Throwing Appliance: A device that fires a line to another ship or to a person in rescue operations.
DPA (Designated Person Ashore): The person ashore appointed under the ISM Code to link the ship and the company on safety matters.
Katabatik Rüzgâr: A wind caused by cold air flowing downhill under gravity from high ground.
Anabatik Rüzgâr: A wind blowing up a slope that has been warmed by the sun during the day.
Sea Breeze (Deniz Meltemi): A local wind blowing from the sea towards the land in the daytime, because the land warms up faster than the sea.
Land Breeze (Kara Meltemi): A local wind blowing from the land towards the sea at night, because the land cools faster than the sea.
Monsun: A large-scale wind system that reverses its direction with the seasons; strongest over the Indian Ocean.
Mistral: A cold, dry northerly wind blowing from southern France over the Mediterranean.
Poyraz: A cold, dry north-easterly wind in Türkiye; strong in the Marmara and Black Sea regions.
Lodos: A warm, humid southerly or south-westerly wind in Türkiye; strong in the Aegean and Marmara.
Tramontana: A cold northerly or north-westerly wind in the Mediterranean.
Douglas Deniz Durumu Skalası: A scale that grades the state of the sea from 0 to 9 according to wave height.
Tropopoz: The boundary between the troposphere and the stratosphere; the upper limit of the weather.
Bağıl Nem: The amount of water vapour in the air as a percentage of the most it could hold at that temperature.
Sling Psikrometresi: An instrument with a wet and a dry bulb thermometer, whirled in the air to measure relative humidity.
Kümülonimbus (Cb): A towering storm cloud; it produces thunder, lightning, hail and heavy rain.
Sirrus (Ci): A thin, high cloud of ice crystals; usually fair weather, but it can announce an approaching front.
Stratus (St): A low, grey layer of cloud; it gives drizzle and poor visibility.
Okta: The unit for cloud cover: eighths of the sky covered, from 0 (clear) to 8 (overcast).
METAR: The standard coded format for routine weather observations from airports and coastal stations.
Form Factor (1+k): A factor showing how the hull form increases frictional resistance; used in the Holtrop-Mennen method.
Wave Pattern Resistance: The resistance component due to the energy in the ship's wave system.
Appendage Resistance: The extra resistance caused by appendages such as the rudder, fin stabilisers and bilge keels.
Air Resistance: The aerodynamic resistance of the ship's hull and superstructure above water.
Effective Power (PE): The power needed to overcome the ship's resistance at a given speed; PE = R × V.
Delivered Power (PD): The power delivered to the propeller; the power left after the shafting losses.
Quasi-Propulsive Coefficient (QPC): The overall propulsive efficiency; the product of the hull, relative rotative and open water efficiencies.
Open Water Efficiency: The efficiency of the propeller working in open water, without the influence of the hull.
Hull Efficiency: Calculated as (1-t)/(1-w), where t is the thrust deduction fraction and w the wake fraction.
Rudder Area Ratio: The rudder area as a proportion of the underwater lateral area; usually at least about 1.5-2% for good manoeuvrability.
Resistance Test: A towing tank test in which a ship model is towed to measure its resistance.
Propeller Open Water Test: A test of a model propeller in open water conditions to find KT, KQ and η₀.
Self-Propulsion Test: A model test in which the model is driven by its own propeller to simulate service conditions.
Preferential Trip: Automatic disconnection of non-essential loads when a generator is overloaded.
Dead Ship Condition: The condition in which all power is lost; recovery uses the emergency generator and batteries.
Power Management System (PMS): The control system that starts and stops the generators automatically and shares the load between them.
Load Sharing: Generators running in parallel sharing the load equally or in proportion to their ratings.
Synchronization: Connecting an incoming generator to the busbar when its voltage, frequency and phase match.
Reverse Power Protection: A protective relay that trips a generator when it starts to take power from the busbar and run as a motor.
VFD (Variable Frequency Drive): A drive that controls the speed of an electric motor by changing the supply frequency; it saves energy on pumps and fans.
Soft Starter: An electronic circuit that starts an electric motor smoothly by raising the voltage gradually.
Star-Delta Starter: A starting method that runs the motor in star connection and then switches to delta, reducing the starting current.
Megger Test: An insulation resistance test made with a high test voltage; the result is given in MΩ.
Navtex Receiver: A receiver that automatically picks up navigational and meteorological warnings on 518 kHz and prints or displays them.
S-Band / X-Band Radar: S-band (10 cm): longer range and better performance in rain. X-band (3 cm): higher resolution and detects SARTs.
Gyro Repeater: A compass repeater driven by the master gyrocompass, used to read the heading and take bearings at other positions.
BNWAS: Bridge Navigational Watch Alarm System; a mandatory system that checks at intervals that the officer of the watch is alert.
MARPOL Ek I: Prevention of pollution by oil; requires, among other things, the Oil Record Book and an oil filtering system.
MARPOL Ek II: Rules for the prevention of pollution by noxious liquid substances carried in bulk.
MARPOL Ek III: Prevention of pollution by harmful substances carried by sea in packaged form.
MARPOL Ek IV: Rules for the prevention of pollution by sewage from ships.
MARPOL Ek V: Prevention of pollution by garbage from ships; stricter discharge bans apply in special areas.
MARPOL Ek VI: Prevention of air pollution from ships; limits on SOx, NOx and CO₂ emissions.
ECA (Emission Control Area): A sea area where fuel sulphur must not exceed 0.10% (SOx ECA) and/or NOx Tier III limits apply (NOx ECA).
SECA: Sulphur Emission Control Area; the sulphur content of fuel used is limited to 0.10%.
NECA: NOx Emission Control Area; an area where the Tier III NOx limits apply.
SIRE (Ship Inspection Report): The inspection programme for tankers and gas carriers run by OCIMF.
CDI (Chemical Distribution Institute): The inspection programme for chemical tankers and terminals.
Rightship: A vetting and safety rating programme, mainly for dry bulk carriers.
IHM (Inventory of Hazardous Materials): The document listing the hazardous materials on board, required by the Hong Kong Convention and the EU Ship Recycling Regulation.
Continuous Synopsis Record (CSR): A record of the ship's history of name, flag, owners and class; required by SOLAS Chapter XI-1.
SMS (Safety Management System): The company's and ship's system of safety policies and procedures under the ISM Code.
Warping: Moving the ship along the berth with her mooring lines, using her own winches or shore assistance.
Kedging: Moving a ship by laying out a small (kedge) anchor and heaving in on it.
Stern First Approach: Approaching the berth stern first; used in confined areas and for Mediterranean mooring.
Wheel Over Point (WOP): The point at which the rudder must be put over to make an alteration of course, worked out from the ship's advance and transfer.
Dragging Anchor: The anchor fails to hold the seabed and drags; it requires an alarm and immediate action.
Holding Ground: How well the seabed holds the anchor: mud and sand hold well, rock and coral poorly.
Scope (Zincir Uzunluğu): The ratio of the length of cable paid out to the depth of water; about 5 to 7 times is recommended for good holding.
Let Go (Demir Bırak): The order to release the windlass brake so that the anchor drops to the seabed.
Short Stay: While heaving up, the anchor cable has been shortened and leads steeply down; the stage before 'up and down'.
Long Stay: The anchor cable is long and leads out nearly horizontally; a sign that the anchor is holding well.
Breast Line: A mooring line led at right angles to the ship's centreline; it stops the ship moving off the berth.
Spring Line: A mooring line led diagonally that stops the ship moving ahead or astern along the berth; there are forward and after springs.
Head Line: A mooring line led forward from the bow to the berth.
Stern Line: A mooring line led aft from the stern to the berth.
Bow Stopper: The fitting on the forecastle that locks the anchor cable and takes its load off the windlass.
Single Up: The order before departure to reduce the moorings to one line at each position.
All Fast: The report that all mooring lines are made fast; the berthing operation is complete.
Stand By Engine: The order to the engine room to get the engine ready for manoeuvring.
Finished With Engine (FWE): The telegraph order that the engine is no longer required; usually given after the ship has berthed or anchored.
